items.readable_text:
Content:
When the characteristic equation of a Cauchy-Euler equation has the complex roots [MATH: \lambda = a \pm b \textrm{i},] the general solution is

Content:
[MATH: y(t) = A t^{a + b \textrm{i}} + A t^{a - b \textrm{i}}.]

Content:
For example, if the complex roots are [MATH: \lambda = 2 \pm 3 \textrm{i},] then the general solution is

Content:
[MATH: y(t) = A t^{2 + 3 \textrm{i}} + B t^{2 - 3 \textrm{i}}.]

Content:
However, we can simplify this form of the general solution even further using Euler's formula. To start, let's focus on [MATH: t^{2+3\textrm{i}}] and separate it into a product:

Content:
[MATH: t^{2+3\textrm{i}} = t^{2} t^{3\textrm{i}}]

Content:
Now, using the rules of logarithms, we have that

Content:
[MATH: t^{3\textrm{i}} = e^{\ln t^{3\textrm{i}} } = e^{3\textrm{i} \ln t}.]

Content:
Then, using Euler's formula, we have

Content:
[MATH: e^{3\textrm{i} \ln t} = e^{\textrm{i} \cdot 3 \ln t} = \cos (3 \ln t) + \textrm{i} \sin (3 \ln t).]

Content:
So, we have that
[MATH: t^{2+3\textrm{i}} = t^2 \left( \cos (3 \ln t) + \textrm{i} \sin (3 \ln t) \right).]

Content:
By the same reasoning,

Content:
[MATH: t^{2 − 3\textrm{i}}|= t^{2}(\cos (− 3\ln t) + \textrm{i}\sin (− 3\ln t)); = t^{2}(\cos (3\ln t) − \textrm{i}\sin (3\ln t)).]

Content:
Therefore, the general solution can be expressed as

Content:
[MATH: y(t)|= At^{2 + 3\textrm{i}} + Bt^{2 − 3\textrm{i}}; = At^{2}(\cos (3\ln t) + \textrm{i}\sin (3\ln t)) + Bt^{2}(\cos (3\ln t) − \textrm{i}\sin (3\ln t)); = t^{2}((A + B)\cos (3\ln t) + \textrm{i}(A − B)\sin (3\ln t)).]

Content:
Finally, we can rewrite [MATH: y(t)] as

Content:
[MATH: y(t) = t^{2} \left( c_1 \cos( 3 \ln{t} ) + c_2 \sin( 3 \ln{t} ) \right),]
where [MATH: c_1 = A+B] and [MATH: c_2 = \textrm{i}(A-B).]

sections.normalized_html:
Find the general solution to the equation

[MATH: x^2 y'' + xy' + 4y = 0,\quad x > 0.]
sections.readable_text:
Find the general solution to the equation

[MATH: x^2 y'' + xy' + 4y = 0,\quad x > 0.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
This is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume the solutions take the form [MATH: y=x^\lambda.] Differentiating [MATH: y] with respect to [MATH: x] gives

[MATH: y' = \lambda x^{\lambda -1}, \qquad y'' = \lambda(\lambda-1)x^{\lambda-2}]

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

[MATH: x^{2} ⋅ λ(λ − 1)x^{λ − 2} + x ⋅ λx^{λ − 1} + 4x^{λ}|= 0; λ(λ − 1)x^{λ} + λx^{λ} + 4x^{λ}|= 0; x^{λ}[λ(λ − 1) + λ + 4]|= 0.]

So, we have the following characteristic equation:

[MATH: λ(λ − 1) + λ + 4|= 0; λ^{2} + 4|= 0; λ^{2}|= − 4; λ|= ± 2\textrm{i}]

Therefore, the general solution is

[MATH: y(x)=c_1 \cos( 2 \ln{x} ) + c_2\sin( 2 \ln{x} ).]

Determine the general solution to the equation

[MATH: t^2 y'' +5ty'+8y = 0,\quad t\gt 0.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
This is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume the solutions take the form [MATH: y=t^\lambda.] Differentiating [MATH: y] with respect to [MATH: t] gives

[MATH: y' = \lambda t^{\lambda -1}, \qquad y'' = \lambda(\lambda-1)t^{\lambda-2}.]

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

[MATH: t^{2} ⋅ λ(λ − 1)t^{λ − 2} + 5t ⋅ λt^{λ − 1} + 8t^{λ}|= 0; λ(λ − 1)t^{λ} + 5λt^{λ} + 8t^{λ}|= 0; t^{λ}[λ(λ − 1) + 5λ + 8]|= 0.]

So, we have the following characteristic equation:

[MATH: λ(λ − 1) + 5λ + 8|= 0; λ^{2} + 4λ + 8|= 0]

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

[MATH: λ^{2} + 4λ + 8|= 0; (λ^{2} + 4λ + 4) − 4 + 8|= 0; (λ + 2)^{2}|= − 4; λ + 2|= ± 2\textrm{i}; λ|= − 2 ± 2\textrm{i}]

Therefore, the general solution is

[MATH: y(t) = t^{-2} \left( c_1 \cos( 2 \ln{t} ) + c_2 \sin( 2 \ln{t} ) \right).]

[MATH: x^2 y'' + xy' + 49 y = 0]

has the general solution

[MATH: y(x)= c_1 \cos(7 \ln{x} ) + c_2\sin(7 \ln{x} ),]

solve the initial value problem

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We find the constants [MATH: c_1] and [MATH: c_2] using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting [MATH: y(1) = 0] into the general solution gives [MATH: 0 = c_1.]

  • To apply the condition [MATH: y'(1) = -7,] we first differentiate [MATH: y] to get [MATH: y^{′}|= (7)/(x)(c_{2}\cos (7\ln x) − c_{1}\sin (7\ln x)).] Then, we substitute [MATH: y'(1) = -7] and [MATH: c_1 = 0] into the above to get [MATH: − 7|= 7c_{2}; c_{2}|= − 1.]

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is [MATH: y(x) = -\sin(7 \ln{x} ).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When the characteristic equation of a Cauchy-Euler equation has the complex roots [MATH: \lambda = a \pm b \textrm{i},] the general solution is

Content:
[MATH: y(t) = A t^{a + b \textrm{i}} + A t^{a - b \textrm{i}}.]

Content:
For example, if the complex roots are [MATH: \lambda = 2 \pm 3 \textrm{i},] then the general solution is

Content:
[MATH: y(t) = A t^{2 + 3 \textrm{i}} + B t^{2 - 3 \textrm{i}}.]

Content:
However, we can simplify this form of the general solution even further using Euler's formula. To start, let's focus on [MATH: t^{2+3\textrm{i}}] and separate it into a product:

Content:
[MATH: t^{2+3\textrm{i}} = t^{2} t^{3\textrm{i}}]

Content:
Now, using the rules of logarithms, we have that

Content:
[MATH: t^{3\textrm{i}} = e^{\ln t^{3\textrm{i}} } = e^{3\textrm{i} \ln t}.]

Content:
Then, using Euler's formula, we have

Content:
[MATH: e^{3\textrm{i} \ln t} = e^{\textrm{i} \cdot 3 \ln t} = \cos (3 \ln t) + \textrm{i} \sin (3 \ln t).]

Content:
So, we have that
[MATH: t^{2+3\textrm{i}} = t^2 \left( \cos (3 \ln t) + \textrm{i} \sin (3 \ln t) \right).]

Content:
By the same reasoning,

Content:
[MATH: t^{2 − 3\textrm{i}}|= t^{2}(\cos (− 3\ln t) + \textrm{i}\sin (− 3\ln t)); = t^{2}(\cos (3\ln t) − \textrm{i}\sin (3\ln t)).]

Content:
Therefore, the general solution can be expressed as

Content:
[MATH: y(t)|= At^{2 + 3\textrm{i}} + Bt^{2 − 3\textrm{i}}; = At^{2}(\cos (3\ln t) + \textrm{i}\sin (3\ln t)) + Bt^{2}(\cos (3\ln t) − \textrm{i}\sin (3\ln t)); = t^{2}((A + B)\cos (3\ln t) + \textrm{i}(A − B)\sin (3\ln t)).]

Content:
Finally, we can rewrite [MATH: y(t)] as

Content:
[MATH: y(t) = t^{2} \left( c_1 \cos( 3 \ln{t} ) + c_2 \sin( 3 \ln{t} ) \right),]
where [MATH: c_1 = A+B] and [MATH: c_2 = \textrm{i}(A-B).]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Shortcut for Cauchy-Euler Equations with Complex Roots

Content:
In general, if the characteristic equation of a Cauchy-Euler equation has imaginary roots [MATH: \lambda = a \pm b\textrm{i},] then the general solution is

Content:
[MATH: y(x) = Ax^{a+b\textrm{i}} + B x^{a-b\textrm{i}}.]

Content:
Using Euler's formula, the above can be simplified to

Content:
[MATH: y(t) = x^a \left( c_1 \cos(b \ln x) + c_2 \sin(b \ln x) \right)]

Content:
where [MATH: c_1 = A+B] and [MATH: c_2=\textrm{i} (A-B).]

---

Item 3 — Example: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots

Example Prompt:
Find the general solution to the equation

[MATH: x^2 y'' + xy' + 4y = 0,\quad x > 0.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
This is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume the solutions take the form [MATH: y=x^\lambda.] Differentiating [MATH: y] with respect to [MATH: x] gives

[MATH: y' = \lambda x^{\lambda -1}, \qquad y'' = \lambda(\lambda-1)x^{\lambda-2}]

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

[MATH: x^{2} ⋅ λ(λ − 1)x^{λ − 2} + x ⋅ λx^{λ − 1} + 4x^{λ}|= 0; λ(λ − 1)x^{λ} + λx^{λ} + 4x^{λ}|= 0; x^{λ}[λ(λ − 1) + λ + 4]|= 0.]

So, we have the following characteristic equation:

[MATH: λ(λ − 1) + λ + 4|= 0; λ^{2} + 4|= 0; λ^{2}|= − 4; λ|= ± 2\textrm{i}]

Therefore, the general solution is

[MATH: y(x)=c_1 \cos( 2 \ln{x} ) + c_2\sin( 2 \ln{x} ).]

---

Item 6 — Example: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots

Example Prompt:

[MATH: t^2 y'' +5ty'+8y = 0,\quad t\gt 0.]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
This is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume the solutions take the form [MATH: y=t^\lambda.] Differentiating [MATH: y] with respect to [MATH: t] gives

[MATH: y' = \lambda t^{\lambda -1}, \qquad y'' = \lambda(\lambda-1)t^{\lambda-2}.]

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

[MATH: t^{2} ⋅ λ(λ − 1)t^{λ − 2} + 5t ⋅ λt^{λ − 1} + 8t^{λ}|= 0; λ(λ − 1)t^{λ} + 5λt^{λ} + 8t^{λ}|= 0; t^{λ}[λ(λ − 1) + 5λ + 8]|= 0.]

So, we have the following characteristic equation:

[MATH: λ(λ − 1) + 5λ + 8|= 0; λ^{2} + 4λ + 8|= 0]

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

[MATH: λ^{2} + 4λ + 8|= 0; (λ^{2} + 4λ + 4) − 4 + 8|= 0; (λ + 2)^{2}|= − 4; λ + 2|= ± 2\textrm{i}; λ|= − 2 ± 2\textrm{i}]

Therefore, the general solution is

[MATH: y(t) = t^{-2} \left( c_1 \cos( 2 \ln{t} ) + c_2 \sin( 2 \ln{t} ) \right).]
